=== key e892145e69ba
Kind of decision: which experiment or hypothesis to pursue
Problem: Which frontier model to use as the teacher for rationale generation.
Write-up text before the decision: the judge step. Samples which have unparseable responses or score are retried, and sample where the final scores disagree with the ground truth class are regenerated with ground truth conditioning with upto $3$ retries. We then judge the generated samples using Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the judge model based on an evidence grounded judge specific rubric based prompt (See Section K) judging on score calibration, observation specificity, innocent-interpretation quality, misaligned-interpretation quality, conclusion quality, and internal consistency. The judge emits a detailed rationale along with a final summarized score in $[0,10]$ which we filter by $\gamma{=}7$ threshold, and then select best-of-$N$ per sample to have a high-quality rationales target for supervision. Samples where no candidates generations pass the threshold are dropped to maintain quality. ### F.2 Model choice for teacher rationale generation The rationale generation step in our pipeline is critical for internalizing the teacher’s reasoning patterns, so any miscalibration in the teacher’s generated rationales propagates directly into the trained monitor as well. We therefore evaluate four frontier reasoning models as candidate teachers via prompting using our scheming specification $\mathbf{S}$: Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4. Since our methodology (Section D) consists of a ground-truth conditioned regeneration step for rationales with incorrect scores, we primarily focus on score alignment with the rubric and reasoning quality as the key factors for selecting a teacher model.

=== key 0625b8d2e7bf
Kind of decision: whether to continue or drop a line of work
Problem: Whether Qwen3-8B could serve as its own teacher instead of a frontier model.
Write-up text before the decision: tself. The student model that we intend to use for fine-tuning is also Qwen3-8B, hence the only difference from our methodology is the teacher model. The two variants where (i) Using a frontier model as the teacher, and (ii) using the self model Qwen3-8B as the teacher, we generate rationales using the scheming specification over the same training dataset all with 8688 prompts. We then regenerate the prompts with incorrect binary scheming score, and filter using the same Claude Sonnet 4.5 models as the judge with the threshold-$7$ judge filter. After filtering the prompts, and selecting per-sample best-of-$N$ rationales, the frontier variant yields 8,688 balanced training rows with at least one high-quality rationale per training prompt, whereas the self-generation variant yields only 384 filtered examples. We assess the gap along three axes: - Format compliance. Qwen3-8B produces format-compliant rationales at 76–100% across datasets, hence format compliance is not the bottleneck. - Judge pass rate is low. Only 11.9% of Qwen3-8B’s rationales score $\geq 7$ from the judge, vs. $\sim 26\%$ for the frontier teacher. The judge scores reasoning and calibration, hence the gap is primarily about the score that the Qwen3-8B model assigns, and how it argues. - Verdict accuracy is low. Three rounds of ground-truth-conditioned regeneration recover only 69.8% of incorrect Qwen3-8B rationales, vs. almost full recovery of 97.2% for the frontier variant. The resulting training data of 384 rows from a $33{,}604$-prompt budget is too few to train a competitive monitor under our recipe.

=== key 04de1cbefbe1
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: How to interpret and state the non-monotonic effect of broader training mixtures.
Write-up text before the decision: ing mixes appear to somewhat improve final OOD transfer, especially with Bash variants, although intermediate additions are not monotonic. To study how training data breadth affects OOD generalization, we start from training on STRIDE and progressively add Gloom, CoT-Red-Handed, and Bash variants (BashArena and BashBench) to the training mixture (all), and train a separate SFT model (starting from the base checkpoint) for each mixture. This produces a sequence of cumulative training mixtures that expand both the domain coverage and the behavioral coverage of misalignment. STRIDE primarily covers egregious scheming in synthetic enterprise software engineering settings, Gloom adds additional scheming style operational settings, CoT-Red-Handed adds covert coding sabotage, and the Bash variants add multi-turn shell and systems agent sabotage. Figure 5 shows the cumulative mixture composition and the resulting Mean-OOD pAUROC@20 for SFT-trained Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B monitors. We observe that the overall trend supports the breadth hypothesis although not in a strictly monotonic way (see Figure 5). For Qwen3-8B, we see marginal improvements in Mean-OOD pAUROC@20 after adding Gloom, although adding CoT-Red-Handed improves it further, i.e. by $5.6$ percentage points (p.p.). The Bash variants take that further by a rise of $11.5$ p.p., reaching a final Mean-OOD pAUROC@20 of $0.610$. For Qwen3-32B, the performance regresses after adding Gloom, but more than compensates with the addition of CoT-Red-Handed and finally reaches a final Mean-OOD pAUROC@20 of $0.668$ with Bash variants.

=== key c3ab1011881d
Kind of decision: which experiment or hypothesis to pursue
Problem: What RL reward design to use.
Write-up text before the decision: $\mathcal{D}_{\text{RL}}$ is obtained by stripping the assistant completions from the SFT dataset, having only labelled prompts $(\tau_{i},y_{i})$ without the assistant completions. We use GRPO with prompt batch size $32$ and group size $G{=}4$ rollouts per prompt, however with the pairwise ranking reward, each training group contains one positive and one negative prompt with $G$ rollouts for each, hence the effective group size is $2G$ sampled completions. We checkpoint every $20$ optimizer steps and select RL checkpoints using the validation pAUROC@20, with the OOD datasets held out for evaluation on the best checkpoint selected from validation. Every rollout is parsed for a final score $\hat{s}\in\{0,\ldots,10\}$ and normalized to $\hat{p}=\hat{s}/10$. As previously defined, our total reward consists of the Brier reward $r^{\mathrm{Brier}}_{ig}$ which calibrates the normalized score to the binary labels, and $r^{\mathrm{pair}}_{ig}$ is the pairwise-matrix ranking reward which directly optimizes the ranking boundary. Particularly, random positives and negatives are paired across the entire training mixture which encourages global separation such that a scheming example from any source should outrank a benign example from any other source. This binary objective is aligned with AUROC/pAUROC evaluation, but it is not an ordinal severity objective since all positive examples share the same target $y=1$. Our goal in this work was to test the initial hypothesis that a lightweight RL refinement stage can improve action-only monitoring performance beyond supervised distillation.
